design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; no protocol or registration mentioned) of how side-effects of ketamine were assessed and reported in studies of adults with unipolar or bipolar depression who received at least one dose by any route, with a change in depression as the study's primary outcome. MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Database searched from 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, no language limit. 60 studies (20 randomized trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case reports or series, 3 retrospective studies; 899 patients given ketamine) were synthesized qualitatively by counting how many studies assessed and reported each category of side-effect (psychiatric, psychotomimetic or dissociative, cardiovascular, neurological or cognitive, other) over three time frames: acute (within 4 hours of a single dose), cumulative (after repeated doses) and long-term (at least 2 weeks after the last dose). A planned meta-analysis was dropped. The PDF read is the online-first version (Lancet Psychiatry, published online 27 July 2017), paginated 1 to 14.
can_establish: Which side-effects were reported in depression studies of ketamine published up to 2016, in how many studies, over which time frames, and how often harms were actively and systematically assessed rather than recorded only when patients mentioned them.
cannot_establish: How often any side-effect occurs (no incidence figures are extracted or pooled), how much more often it occurs with ketamine than with placebo (no comparative data are given), whether side-effects depend on dose (doses are not tabulated), or what happens with long-term repeated use (rarely assessed in the included studies); the statements about urinary, liver, cognitive and dependence harms in other populations come from literature outside the systematic search.

sample.recruitment: Database search (MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, Cochrane Database), 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, terms combining ketamine with depression, affective, mood or bipolar and with safe, side or adverse; plus 23 records from unspecified other sources; letters reporting a case were eligible (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF). The settings of the included studies are not tabulated; Table 1 gives each study's design, number given ketamine, route and single or multiple dosing, but not setting, diagnosis mix or dose.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with a validated diagnosis of unipolar or bipolar depression given one or more doses of ketamine by any route, frequency and time course, in studies reporting change in depression as a primary outcome. Excluded: animal studies; non-original or mechanistic reports; studies of children or adolescents only; studies whose primary interest was another disorder (pain, fibromyalgia, suicidality, PTSD, recreational drug use) unless a patient with depression was included; studies with ECT as a concomitant intervention; studies of other NMDA-receptor antagonists only (nitrous oxide, MK-0657, AZD6765) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated by study. Routes (Table 2): intravenous 49 articles, about 737 patients (214 given multiple doses); oral 6 articles, 72 patients; intramuscular 3, 7; subcutaneous 4, 25; intranasal 2, 18; sublingual 1, 26; transmucosal 1, 17; total 902, with 3 patients counted under two routes; the authors call these numbers approximate (p. 7 of the online-first PDF).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Withdrawals within studies are summarized by reason (pp. 6–7 of the online-first PDF).
sample.selection_effects: Selection required depression change as a primary outcome, so dedicated safety studies and harms reported only in separate safety papers could be missed. Most included studies were uncontrolled (about three-fifths had no placebo or control, by the editors' reading of the Figure 2 pie chart) and most patients received a single intravenous dose. Table 1 footnotes flag possible sample overlap between several studies from the same groups, so the total of 899 patients may count some people more than once.

exposure.measurement: As given in the primary studies; the review records route and whether dosing was single or multiple, but not the dose (pp. 3–6 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as tabulated: mostly single intravenous doses; multiple doses in about 356 of 899 patients; non-intravenous routes (oral, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intranasal, sublingual, transmucosal) in 17 route entries (Table 2, p. 7 of the online-first PDF). Most studies used racemic ketamine (p. 11 of the online-first PDF).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Concomitant medication was among the data the authors say they collected, but it is not reported in the article (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).

comparison.controls: Whatever the primary studies used: placebo, active control, dose comparison, or none; most studies had no placebo or control group (Figure 2, p. 7 of the online-first PDF).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Health screening before ketamine and pre-existing medical illness were among the data collected, but the authors state it is unclear in many studies whether comprehensive health screening was done (p. 10 of the online-first PDF); no study-level data are shown.

outcomes.instruments: The review's outcome is the reporting of side-effects: for each study and each of four categories, the period assessed (short term within 4 hours, cumulative, long term at least 2 weeks after the last dose), the measures used (for example BPRS, CADSS, YMRS, SAFTEE, PRISE, vital signs, liver function tests) and whether reporting was systematic (presence and absence reported) or ad hoc (only when present), and whether assessment was active or passive (Methods › Analysis; Table 1, pp. 2–6 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.validity_norms: Each article was appraised with a relevant appraisal checklist or tool reported in the appendix (p. 2 of the online-first PDF); the appendix was not read and no appraisal results appear in the article.
outcomes.operationalization: A side-effect counted as having occurred if a study listed it in at least one patient (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). Results are therefore numbers of studies reporting a side-effect, not numbers of patients affected.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; the synthesis consists of counts and proportions of studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Study selection by two authors with consensus and a senior author for discrepancies; data collected by two authors and extracted by four, without a stated duplicate-extraction procedure (pp. 2, 11 of the online-first PDF).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review counts studies: acute side-effects assessed in 55 of 60 (92%), cumulative in 24 (40%), long-term in 12 (20%); acute psychiatric side-effects described in 23 (38%) studies, psychotomimetic or dissociative in 43 (72%), acute cardiovascular changes in 23 (38%), other side-effects in 32 (53%); urinary side-effects assessed in 5 studies, liver function tests in 7 (abnormal in 2), questions about dependence in 2; systematic reporting of psychiatric or psychotomimetic side-effects in 25 (42%), cardiovascular in 19 (32%), neurological or cognitive in 14 (23%) and other in 14 (23%) (pp. 6–8 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. Two study-level comparisons are reported descriptively: intravenous against other routes, and randomized trials against other designs (pp. 7–8 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA reporting is stated. A meta-analysis was planned and then judged inappropriate after data extraction because of clinical diversity, varied routes, doses and comparators, and reporting differences (p. 6 of the online-first PDF).
analysis.selective_reporting: The study-level appraisal is placed in an appendix and never used in the text. Doses are not tabulated, so side-effects cannot be related to dose. The statement that side-effects were reported more often with ketamine than placebo in controlled studies is given without numbers. Figures 2, 4 and 5 present some counts only graphically.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 60 studies of ketamine in depression published from 1999 to 2016, most of them without a control group and most patients given a single intravenous dose, acute side-effects were assessed in almost all, but cumulative effects in 40% and long-term effects in 20%; harms were often recorded passively and reported ad hoc; urinary symptoms were assessed in 5 studies, liver function in 7 and dependence in 2. The most often reported side-effects were headache, dizziness, dissociation, raised blood pressure and blurred vision; psychiatric and psychotomimetic effects and cardiovascular changes were described as short-lived. Withdrawals for side-effects were few and are given as counts of participants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary states that after acute dosing, psychiatric, psychotomimetic, cardiovascular, neurological and other side-effects were reported more frequently after ketamine than after placebo, and that the findings suggest a selective reporting bias (p. 1 of the online-first PDF). The comparison with placebo is asserted in one sentence of the Results without any counts (p. 6). The selective-reporting conclusion is supported by the review's own analysis of how harms were assessed. The Discussion and Conclusion then list urological, hepatic, cognitive and dependence harms reported with high-dose or repeated use in people with chronic pain and in people who use ketamine recreationally (pp. 9–11); these come from a narrative selection outside the systematic search and are cited for the risk of long-term use in depression, which the included studies did not measure. The authors state clearly that only single-dose acute effects could be judged (p. 8).

timeline.event: Berman et al.: the initial pilot placebo-controlled trial, as this review calls it, included here as one of the 20 randomized trials (listed with 7 patients given ketamine and short-term BPRS and VAS ratings).
This review: the authors describe it as the first systematic review of the safety of ketamine in depression after single and repeated doses.
Beck et al.: meta-analysis of BPRS and PANSS ratings after single doses in healthy volunteers (a different population; this round's first-pass card sc_beck_2020).
Dean et al.: Cochrane review of randomized trials of ketamine and other glutamate modulators in unipolar depression (this round's first-pass card sc_dean_2021).

Anand et al.: randomized trial of six ketamine infusions against ECT in 365 analysed patients, reporting moderate and severe adverse events by arm and rating dissociation on every treatment day (CADSS values in its supplement).

replication.where_it_stands: The review documents that the early ketamine-for-depression literature measured harms of repeated or long-term use poorly; it cannot give rates. Later randomized trials and reviews on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023; Anand et al., 2023) report adverse events more systematically, and the authors' group announced a Ketamine Side Effect Tool and a Ketamine Safety Screening Tool (p. 10 of the online-first PDF).

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: C K Loo declares fees for attending a Janssen Advisory Board meeting; all other authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests, p. 11 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the New South Wales Institute of Psychiatry, the School of Psychiatry of the University of New South Wales, the Black Dog Institute, St George and Wesley Hospitals (Sydney) and the University of Otago. Several included studies come from the senior author's group (for example Loo et al., 2016; Galvez et al., 2014; George et al.), and three authors were developing the Ketamine Side Effect Tool that the review recommends (Contributors, p. 11). Janssen was developing esketamine, the S-isomer whose large trials the review notes were under way (p. 11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of repeated ketamine dosing in depression with a structured, pre-specified harms protocol (active questioning at each dose and for months afterwards, including urinary symptoms, liver tests, cognitive testing against a control group and assessment of craving and dependence), reporting numbers of patients affected per arm, and an individual-participant meta-analysis of harms across existing trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, intervention and the harms of interest are described, but no comparator is specified, and the outcome criterion for inclusion is depression change rather than side-effects.
No protocol or registration is mentioned; the planned meta-analysis was abandoned after extraction.
All designs were included because trials are unlikely to detect rare or long-term harms (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).

Four databases, the search terms printed, no language restriction, and a search ending about 7 months before online publication; but no trial registries, no stated reference-list or expert searching, and the 23 records from other sources are not described.
Two authors screened and assessed full texts, settling disputes by consensus and discrepancies with a senior author (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
Two authors collected and four extracted data (Contributors), but no duplicate extraction or consensus procedure is described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow diagram gives reasons for the 35 excluded full texts by category only; no list of excluded studies is given or referred to.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, number given ketamine, route, single or multiple dosing and side-effect measures, but not the population (diagnosis, age, setting), the dose or the comparator of each study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article says each study was appraised with a relevant checklist or tool given in the appendix, which was not read; no appraisal results appear in the text. The review separately applied the Cochrane Adverse Effects Methods Group checks (selective outcome reporting, withdrawals, presence of a control group).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Meta-analysis planned and then judged inappropriate (p. 6 of the online-first PDF).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation rests on the weaknesses of the primary studies' harms assessment (no control group in most, passive monitoring, ad hoc reporting, short follow-up), and the authors limit their conclusions to single-dose acute effects.
Clinical and reporting diversity is described as the reason for not pooling, and route (intravenous against other) and design (randomized against other) are compared descriptively.
No quantitative synthesis; within-study selective reporting of harms is the review's subject.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Conflicts are declared (one author with Janssen advisory-board fees), but the review's funding source is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (no protocol, item 2; no list of excluded studies, item 7), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2 whatever the provisional item 9 turns out to be. For this review the rating says less than usual about usefulness: its question is how harms were measured, and its main finding (harms of repeated and long-term use were rarely assessed in depression studies up to 2016) follows directly from Table 1 and the counts in the Results, which a reader can check. It may be cited for the counts of studies assessing and reporting each category and time frame of side-effect, for the list of most commonly reported side-effects, for the withdrawal counts and for the scarcity of urinary, liver, cognitive and dependence assessment; it may not be cited for incidence of any side-effect, for a ketamine-placebo difference, for dose-dependence, or for the harms in other populations described in its Discussion, which must be cited to their primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Searches of MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and the Cochrane Database for articles published 1 January 1999 to 30 December 2016, without language restriction, with depression change as a required primary outcome; the initial database search was run independently by three authors.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Study flow: 568 records from databases and 23 from other sources, 591 screened; 303 met exclusion criteria and 186 did not meet inclusion criteria; 103 records included; 95 full texts assessed and 35 excluded (26 non-original research, 5 other primary disorders, 1 animal, 1 paediatric, 1 concomitant ECT, 1 other NMDA antagonists); 60 studies included: 20 randomized trials, 17 open-label trials, 20 case series or reports, 3 retrospective studies.

The 60 studies included 899 patients who received at least one dose of ketamine; by route, intravenous 49 articles and 737 patients, oral 6 and 72, intramuscular 3 and 7, subcutaneous 4 and 25, intranasal 2 and 18, sublingual 1 and 26, transmucosal 1 and 17 (total 902, 3 patients counted under two routes); about 356 received multiple doses. The 20 randomized trials together included 430 participants given ketamine.
key_findings.note: The authors call the per-route numbers approximations, and Table 1 footnotes flag possible sample overlap between several studies, so 899 may count some patients twice.

key_findings.finding: Acute side-effects were assessed in 55 (92%) studies, cumulative side-effects in 24 (40%) and long-term side-effects (at least 2 weeks after the last dose) in 12 (20%); most study reports had no placebo or control group. In studies with a placebo or comparator, side-effects in all categories were said to be reported more commonly with ketamine, without numbers.

Acute psychiatric side-effects were described in 23 (38%) studies and psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects in 43 (72%); score changes were generally self-limiting. The most common psychiatric side-effect was anxiety, followed by agitation or irritability, euphoria or mood elevation, delusions or unusual thoughts, panic and apathy; when delayed symptoms (anxiety, worsening depression or suicidality, hypomania) occurred, their link to ketamine was unclear.

Psychiatric reasons for withdrawal across all studies: worsening mood (12 participants), anxiety (6), suicidal ideation (5), panic attack (2), irritability (1); one suicide attempt was reported in one study; dissociation was the only psychotomimetic reason for withdrawal (2 participants); 5 patients were withdrawn for cardiovascular side-effects.

Dissociation was the most commonly reported psychotomimetic side-effect, followed by perceptual disturbance, odd sensations, derealisation, hallucinations, feeling strange or unreal, and depersonalisation; no long-term psychotomimetic effects were reported, but most studies assessed them only within about 4 hours of the dose. Absence of psychosis or mania was reported in 5 (8%) studies and absence of psychotomimetic or dissociative effects in 5 (8%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (end, top of p. 7) and 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies giving ketamine intravenously tended to report more psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects: 72% of intravenous studies against 36% of non-intravenous studies.
key_findings.note: The 72% cannot be reconciled with the other counts; see reporting issue 2.

key_findings.finding: Acute cardiovascular changes were reported in 23 (38%) studies, most often raised blood pressure and heart rate, mostly during or immediately after intravenous dosing, generally resolving within 90 minutes.

Headache and dizziness were the most common neurological side-effects; cognitive side-effects (poor memory, poor concentration, confusion) were reported over the short term only, and potential cognitive side-effects were not assessed in most studies. Other side-effects were reported in 32 (53%) studies, most often blurred vision and nausea.

Urinary side-effects were assessed in only 5 studies; liver function tests were reported in 7 studies, 2 of which found abnormalities after dosing; only 2 studies asked about the development of ketamine dependence or abuse; structured scales for other side-effects (such as SAFTEE or PRISE) were used in 15 (25%) studies, and most relied on passive monitoring with little follow-up beyond the acute period.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 7, the 12th continued on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Side-effects were reported systematically (presence and absence) in 25 (42%) studies for psychiatric or psychotomimetic effects, 19 (32%) for cardiovascular, 14 (23%) for neurological or cognitive and 14 (23%) for other side-effects; in randomized trials the common acute side-effects were reported at rates similar to other designs, but long-term risks, cognition, urinary symptoms and dependence were rarely assessed.
key_findings.note: Figure 5 (p. 9; editors' reading, approximate): headache was reported in about 21 studies (11 randomized), dizziness about 20 (11), dissociation about 18 (8), raised blood pressure about 17 (9), urinary tract side-effects 5 (2) and dependency risk 2 (none randomized).

key_findings.finding: The authors summarize ten main findings, including that acute side-effects are common after ketamine, that active assessment and reporting of side-effects in depression trials are inadequate, that most reported side-effects followed intravenous dosing and resolved shortly after the dose, and that conclusions could be drawn only for single-dose acute effects.

A meta-analysis was planned but judged inappropriate after data extraction because of clinical diversity, different routes, doses and comparators, differing reporting methods and reporting bias; a qualitative review was done instead.

The Conclusion states that acute side-effects of single doses in depression are common but generally transient, that high doses and repeated administration have been associated with urological, hepatic, craving or dependence and cognitive harms in people treated for chronic pain and in people who use ketamine recreationally, that these have not been adequately assessed in depression studies, and that the safety of long-term repeated dosing is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The study flow does not add up, and the summary's 288 articles identified and the Discussion's 288 published reports reviewed do not match the 60 studies included (Figure 1: 591 screened, 303 and 186 excluded, 103 records included, 95 full texts assessed). Editors' arithmetic: 591 minus 303 and 186 leaves 102, not 103; the step from 103 records to 95 full texts is unexplained; and 288 equals 591 minus 303.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of reports reviewed should be cited as 60 studies, not 288; the flow cannot be fully audited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 72% of intravenous studies against 36% of non-intravenous studies reporting psychotomimetic or dissociative side-effects. Editors' calculation: with 49 intravenous and 11 non-intravenous studies (Table 2), 72% is not a whole-number fraction of 49 (35 of 49 is 71%, 36 of 49 is 73%); 36% fits 4 of 11, which would leave 39 of 49 intravenous studies (80%) to make up the 43 studies reporting such effects; 72% equals the overall proportion, 43 of 60.
reporting_issues.consequence: The route comparison is probably misprinted, and the intravenous figure may be higher than stated; the direction (more reports with intravenous dosing) is unaffected, but the 72% should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary states that side-effects of every category were reported more frequently after ketamine than after placebo, but the only supporting text is one sentence in the Results without counts of studies, patients or comparisons.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for any ketamine-placebo difference in side-effects; primary trials or later meta-analyses must be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the number of patients who received ketamine as 7 for the first randomized trial (Berman et al.). Editors' cross-check against that paper (berman_2000, p. 353): 8 people had the ketamine day, 7 of whom completed both days. Together with the sample overlaps flagged in the Table 1 footnotes, this suggests the per-study numbers are sometimes analysed rather than exposed patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the total of 899 patients is approximate in both directions.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Discussion, urothelial cell apoptosis is cited to reference 93 (Chu et al., 2008, a Hong Kong clinical series) although reference 95 (Baker et al., 2016) is the study of ketamine-induced apoptosis in urothelial cells; the same reference 93 is cited for prevalence figures from both Spain and Hong Kong (46% and 90%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation errors in the narrative part; the urinary-harm figures must be taken from the primary studies, not from this review.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Short_2018_SideEffectsSR.pdf: the online-first version (Lancet Psychiatry, published online 27 July 2017), paginated 1–14, not the issue pagination (Lancet Psychiatry 5(1), 65–78, per the reference record); anchors cite 'of the online-first PDF'. Read in full: summary, all sections, Figure 1, Tables 1 and 2, Figures 2 to 5 (values read from the rendered pages at 150 dpi, approximate where read from bars), contributors, declaration of interests and references. The online appendix (quality appraisal) was not read.
